title: Carmel
hookLine: the Carmelites trace their spirit to Elijah on Mount Carmel
tomorrow: Four ways to water a garden

cards: A ridge of hills called Carmel runs down toward the sea in the north of Israel.
In the First Book of Kings, this is where the prophet Elijah calls down fire: an altar, a trench full of water, a crowd waiting, and then fire falls and burns up everything, even the water.
Centuries later, tradition says, Christian hermits settled on that same mountain, in small cells near a spring people connected with Elijah. They became the Carmelites.
And the spirit they took from Elijah isn't only the fire. It's also what happened to him next, after he ran.

teach.b: Right after the fire, Elijah is running for his life. The queen has sworn to kill him. He walks into the wilderness, sits under a bush, and asks to die.
An angel wakes him twice with bread and water, and he walks on to Horeb, the mountain of God, and hides in a cave. Then God says, go out and stand on the mountain.

teach.h: NOT IN THE WIND, QUAKE OR FIRE.
teach.b: The King James tells it: "a great and strong wind rent the mountains, and brake in pieces the rocks before the LORD; but the LORD was not in the wind: and after the wind an earthquake; but the LORD was not in the earthquake: And after the earthquake a fire; but the LORD was not in the fire: and after the fire a still small voice."

The prophet who called down fire learns that God isn't in this fire. Hearing the quiet, Elijah wraps his face in his cloak and goes to the mouth of the cave. That's the turn the Carmelites took as theirs.
Carmel is the fire. Horeb is the whisper. A Carmelite life holds both: zeal for God, and long hours of silent prayer in a small room, listening.

teach.h: AFTER THE FIRE, A STILL SMALL VOICE.
teach.b: The Hebrew behind still small voice is hard to put into English: some hear a gentle whisper, others a sound made of thin silence.

teach.h: CARMEL IS FIRE. HOREB IS HUSH.
teach.b: God, in this story, chooses to be found in a hush, by a man worn out and hiding. And the voice asks the question he first heard in the cave: what are you doing here, Elijah?

how: Carmelite friars and nuns keep long periods of silent prayer each day, often alone in a cell or together in chapel, and look to Elijah as a father of their way of life.

o: a desert valley where early monks lived in caves
the cave where Elijah heard God's quiet voice
the mountain of Elijah's fire, home of the first Carmelites

games.q: fire and hush — tap the pairs.
p: wraps his face in his cloak

s: the still small voice comes on Mount Carmel
the fire falls on Carmel. the still small voice comes later, on Horeb, after Elijah runs.
in the story, the LORD is in the fire on Horeb
the text says the LORD was not in the wind, the earthquake or the fire.
Elijah asks to die before he hears the voice
he sits under a bush in the wilderness and asks to die. an angel feeds him and he walks on.

games.q: you're Elijah in the cave. a wind splits rocks, the ground shakes, fire passes. then everything goes quiet. what do you do?
o: stay inside until the noise starts again.
wrap your face in your cloak and go to the cave's mouth.
call down fire to prove you're still a prophet.
games.why: when he hears the still small voice, he wraps his face in his mantle and stands at the entrance. he goes toward the quiet.

practice: Let the noise come first, worries like wind, something unfinished like a quake, anger like fire, and let each pass; you don't have to make the quiet, only wait for it.
If you pray, wait for God as Elijah did, face covered; if not, listen for the smallest sound in the room.
And if, like Elijah under that bush, you ever feel you'd rather not be alive, please call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.

wordCard.voice: Carmel. Elijah's mountain of fire, home of the first Carmelites, who carried his quieter lesson too.

orig.note: Hebrew: stillness, silence; part of the phrase the King James renders a still small voice.

carryVoice: Your line: the still small voice. After the fire comes the hush, and a question. Until tomorrow.
